\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch15-finetune.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Where the accuracy actually came from: months of unlabelled pretraining, then one epoch on 20,000 labelled reviews.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}This is a far more expensive model to run than the bigram classifier, and the clear benefit has to be weighed against that. \textbf{Chapter 18 makes that trade-off explicit}; for now, note that the three points cost roughly four orders of magnitude in compute.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{05}{What makes the Transformer effective?}{A geometric answer, by way of a model from 2013.}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ 2013}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Word2Vec, and the magic vectors}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}At Google in 2013, Tomas Mikolov and colleagues built a pretrained embedding called \textbf{Word2Vec}, much like the continuous bag-of-words embedding of chapter 14. The objective turned \textbf{correlation} relationships between words into \textbf{distance} relationships in an embedding space.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The resulting space did more than capture similarity. It showed a kind of emergent \textit{word arithmetic}:\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{V(king) $-$ V(man) + V(woman) $\approx$ V(queen)}\quotecite{A gender vector nobody trained for}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}There were dozens of such vectors --- a plural vector, a vector from wild animals to their closest pet equivalent. \textbf{The model had not been trained for any of this explicitly.}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 15.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{How much a 2013 toy and a 2024 model have in common}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}On the surface, nothing could seem further from Word2Vec than a large pretrained Transformer that generates fluent language on any topic. And yet:\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3196\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3102\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3102\textwidth}}
\thead{} & \thead{Word2Vec} & \thead{Transformer} \\ \midrule
Goal & Embed tokens in a vector space & Embed tokens in a vector space \\
Learning principle & Tokens that co-occur end up close & Tokens that co-occur end up close \\
Distance function & Cosine distance & Cosine distance \\
Dimensionality & \textasciitilde{}1,000 per word & 1,000 to 10,000 per word \\
\end{itable}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}You might object: a Transformer is trained to predict missing words, not to group tokens in a space. How does that objective relate to maximising dot-products between co-occurring tokens? \hilite{The answer is the attention mechanism.}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ the geometric account}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Attention is embedding-space refinement}
\leadpar{Attention learns a new embedding space by \textbf{linearly recombining} embeddings from a prior space, weighted toward tokens that are already close.}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Because the weighting is a dot product, tokens with high similarity contribute most to each other's new representation. Over training, this \textbf{pulls already-close vectors together} --- turning correlation relationships into proximity relationships.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch15-why-effective.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont A Transformer learns a series of incrementally refined embedding spaces, each recombining elements of the previous one.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ two properties}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Continuous, and interpolative}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{Semantically continuous}
Moving a little in the embedding space changes the human-facing meaning only a little. Word2Vec's space had this property too.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{Semantically interpolative}
The midpoint between two points represents the \textbf{intermediate meaning} --- a direct consequence of each space being built by interpolating vectors from the previous one.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}This is not entirely unlike the brain. The key learning principle there is \textbf{Hebbian learning} --- \textit{neurons that fire together, wire together}. Correlations between firing events become proximity in the network.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
The Transformer, Word2Vec, and the brain all turn correlation relationships into vector-proximity relationships. All three are \hilite{maps of a space of information}.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ the difference in degree}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Vector programs, not vector functions}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Word2Vec is to today's language models as a logistic regression on MNIST pixels is to a state-of-the-art vision model. It was not even a deep network --- a single shallow layer. Today's Transformers stack dozens of attention and feedforward layers with parameter counts in the billions.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}With that representation power, and a more refined autoregressive objective, we are no longer confined to \textbf{linear} transformations like a gender vector.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4324\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.5076\textwidth}}
\thead{Word2Vec could store} & \thead{A large Transformer can store} \\ \midrule
\inlinecode{plural(cat) -> cats} & \inlinecode{write\_this\_in\_style\_of\_shakespeare("...poem...")} \\
\inlinecode{male\_to\_female(king) -> queen} & and \textbf{millions} of such programs \\
\end{itable}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}These are so complex that it is more accurate to call them \textbf{vector programs} than vector functions --- highly nonlinear maps of the latent space onto itself. Not Python programs: no symbolic statements, no step-by-step data processing.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ the database analogy}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A database you can retrieve more from than you put in}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}You can see a Transformer as a database: it stores information you retrieve via the tokens you pass in. Two differences matter enormously.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{It is continuous}
Not discrete entries but a \textbf{curve}. You can move along it to nearby points and interpolate between them --- so you can retrieve much more than was put in.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{It stores programs}
RoBERTa holds facts, places, people, dates, relationships --- but \textbf{primarily} it is a database of vector programs.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[rose]
Interpolation is the same mechanism behind both outcomes: it leads to \textbf{generalization}, and it leads to \textbf{hallucination}. Not all of what you retrieve will be accurate or meaningful.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{This is the single most useful sentence in the chapter for a professional audience. Hallucination is not a bug to be patched out; it is the same property that makes the model useful, observed from the other side.}

\framekicker{Section 15.5 $\cdot$ the honest limit}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Interpolation is not synthesis}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}In the next chapter we push these models to billions of parameters and trillions of words. Their output can feel like magic --- like an intelligent operator sitting inside, pulling the strings.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{These models are \textbf{fundamentally interpolative}. Thanks to attention, they learn an interpolative embedding space for a significant chunk of all text written in English. Wandering that space leads to interesting, unexpected generalizations --- but it cannot synthesize something fundamentally new with anything close to genuine, human-level intelligence.}\quotecite{Section 15.5, closing}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Keep this claim in mind through chapters 16 and 19, where it is tested against much larger models and much stronger claims.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Common failure modes}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Four ways Transformer code goes quietly wrong}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{No causal mask on the decoder}
Training accuracy shoots up, generation produces nothing coherent. The model is reading its own label. \inlinecode{use\_causal\_mask=True}.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{No positional embedding}
The model trains, converges, and scores several points too low with no error message. It is treating your sentences as \textbf{bags of words}.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%


\vskip 4pt

\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Tokenizer mismatched to weights}
Fine-tuning a pretrained backbone with the wrong tokenizer produces near-random performance. Load both from the \textbf{same preset}.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Default learning rate on fine-tuning}
Adam's default is \textasciitilde{}20$\times$ too large for a pretrained backbone and will wash out the representations in the first few batches.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Three of these four produce \textbf{no exception and no warning} --- only a number that is worse than it should be. That is what makes them worth memorising.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{A language model learns p(token | past tokens)} --- and generates text of any length by being called in a loop, output becoming input.
\item \textbf{A masked language model} learns p(token | surrounding tokens), which is better for representing text than for generating it.
\item \textbf{Seq2seq} splits into an encoder that represents the source and a decoder that predicts the target one token at a time.
\item \textbf{Attention} scores by dot product, normalises by softmax, and returns a weighted sum --- giving direct access to any position in a sequence.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter (2 of 2)}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{The Transformer block} is attention (mixes positions, no nonlinearity) plus feedforward (mixes features, has the nonlinearity), with residuals and layer normalization around both.
\item \textbf{Attention is order-blind}, so positional embeddings are not optional --- leaving them out costs several points and raises no error.
\item \textbf{Pretraining then fine-tuning} beat training from scratch decisively: 93.7\% in one epoch against a 90\% ceiling.
\item \textbf{Attention turns correlation into proximity}, building interpolative embedding spaces --- the source of both generalization and hallucination.
\end{isteps}
